opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something we've talked about a fair bit internally. The way I think about it is that Exo is fundamentally about where the compute lives: letting you pool the devices you already own and run serious models locally. But inference by itself isn't the end product. People want to *do* something with those models, and increasingly that something is agentic coding inside their editor.

What I like about ACP is that it's trying to standardize the seam between the editor and the agent, a bit like LSP did for language tooling. If that seam is clean, then a project like ours doesn't have to build bespoke integrations for every editor. We can focus on making the local backend fast and reliable, and let the protocol handle how an agent talks to your workspace.

So I see it as pretty complementary. The appeal is a fully local loop: your editor, your agent, your model, running on hardware sitting on your desk, with none of your code leaving the machine. For a lot of people, especially those working on proprietary codebases, that's the whole point.

That said, I try to be careful about protocol churn. There are a lot of competing standards in the agent space right now: MCP, ACP, various OpenAI-compatible APIs. We don't want to chase every one of them. Our bias is to support whatever lets people plug in with the least friction, and to keep the core of Exo focused on the hard distributed-systems problems. If ACP keeps gaining traction, and it seems to be, then supporting it is a pretty natural step for us.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so ACP — the Agent Client Protocol — is something I actually think is a really natural fit for what Exo is trying to do. The whole premise of Exo is that you've got a bunch of devices sitting around, your laptop, your Mac mini, maybe an old gaming PC, and you want to pool them together and run models locally without going through a cloud API. And the moment you have that, the obvious next question is, okay, what do I actually do with it? And increasingly the answer is agents. People want their coding agent running against the model they're hosting themselves.

So what Zed did with ACP is basically say, look, there's a standard way for an editor to talk to an agent. It handles the session lifecycle, the streaming, tool calls, permissions, all of that plumbing that every agent otherwise reinvents. If Exo speaks that protocol, then anybody using Zed can point their editor at their own cluster and get a coding agent that never leaves their network. That's a pretty compelling story, especially for people who care about privacy or who are just tired of watching their token bills.

The way I think about it architecturally, Exo already has to expose an inference endpoint, and we've leaned on OpenAI-compatible APIs for that because it's what everything expects. ACP sits one layer above. It's less about "give me the next token" and more about "here's a task, go do it, tell me what you're changing." So adding it isn't really about the inference engine, it's about building an agent loop on top that can orchestrate tool use and then surfacing that through the protocol. Honestly a lot of the work is making sure the open models we're running are good enough at tool calling to not fall over, which is more of a model problem than a protocol problem.

The thing I'm a little cautious about is protocol churn. There's MCP, there's ACP, there's whatever gets announced next month, and you can spend all your time chasing integrations instead of making the core thing better. But ACP is small and well-scoped enough that I don't think it's a huge lift, and the payoff of having a real editor integration is pretty big for the project. So I'm pretty positive on it. It's the kind of thing where if someone in the community wants to drive it, I'd be very happy to see that PR.

astra-6.text: I’d think about it in terms of what it unlocks for someone using Exo. If supporting ACP lets them use Exo from Zed without building a separate integration for every editor, that’s appealing. The question is how well the protocol maps onto what Exo needs to expose, and how much complexity the integration adds. I’d start with a small end-to-end workflow, see where the boundaries are, and build from there.

sol-6.1.text: I think it’s an interesting direction. The way I’d frame it is: Exo handles running the models across your devices, and ACP could give an editor like Zed a standard way to interact with an agent using those models. Those are complementary pieces. The distinction I’d want to understand is how much agent functionality Exo should own versus just providing inference for an agent that speaks ACP. I’d be interested in exploring it, but I wouldn’t want to imply we’ve committed to an implementation.
